lesson.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap

steps.title: Create project and parse path
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls` (or your own name), add `clap = { version = "4.5", features = ["derive"] }` to Cargo.toml, and define a `#[derive(Parser)]` Cli struct with `path: Option<PathBuf>` parsed via `Cli::parse()` in main. Run `cargo run -- -h` to see the generated help.

targets.caption: Add clap with the derive feature
Cli struct with an optional path argument
Auto-generated help output

explanations.topic: clap's derive feature makes CLI parsing easy
Using a PathBuf field as the first positional argument
Deriving Parser adds the parse method
Passing args through cargo run with --
Reading the generated usage/arguments/options help

hints: Make sure Cargo.toml has clap with features = ["derive"]; without it the Parser derive won't exist.
Import the trait with `use clap::Parser;` and PathBuf with `use std::path::PathBuf;`.
Put `#[derive(Parser)]` above `struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }`, then call `let cli = Cli::parse();` in main.
Run `cargo run -- -h` — the `--` separates cargo's flags from your program's flags.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the derive feature on clap, causing 'cannot find derive macro Parser'.
Not importing clap::Parser, so Cli::parse() is not found.
Running `cargo run -h`, which shows cargo's help instead of the app's help.
Making path a plain PathBuf instead of Option<PathBuf>, so it becomes required (<PATH> instead of [PATH]).

steps.title: Add version and about metadata
steps.instructions: Add `#[command(version, about, long_about = "best ls command ever")]` above the Cli struct in src/main.rs. Verify with `cargo run -- --version` and `cargo run -- -h`.

targets.caption: Add the command attribute above the Cli struct
Version flag now in help output

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] auto-generates a --version flag from Cargo.toml
long_about text appears in help output
Clap generates CLI boilerplate so you focus on program logic

hints: Clap's struct-level settings go in a #[command(...)] attribute on the struct.
Place it directly under #[derive(Parser)] and above struct Cli.
Use #[command(version, about, long_about = "...")], then run `cargo run -- --version` (note the `--`).
common_mistakes: Running `cargo run --version`, which prints cargo's version instead of your program's
Using #[clap(...)] syntax from older versions, or forgetting the `derive` feature of clap
Putting the attribute on the field or main() instead of the Cli struct
Forgetting the quotes around the long_about string

steps.title: Default path and check existence
steps.instructions: Default the path with `cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."))` and use `path.try_exists()` to print a red "Path does not exist" via owo-colors. Run `cargo run -- some_fake_path`.

targets.caption: Fall back to "." when no path is given
Check whether the path exists
Add the owo-colors crate
Red error for a fake path

explanations.topic: cli.path is an Option, so unwrap it with a default
Defaulting to the current directory like ls
Checking whether a path exists
owo-colors for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the binary in target/debug

hints: cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>. Use unwrap_or to supply PathBuf::from(".") when it is None.
path.try_exists() returns a Result<bool>. Match the Ok case with `if let Ok(does_exist) = ...` and handle the else branch as a read error.
Add owo-colors to Cargo.toml (`cargo add owo-colors`), import `owo_colors::OwoColorize`, then call `"Path does not exist".red()` inside println!.
Run `cargo run -- some_fake_path`. The `--` separates cargo's arguments from your program's arguments.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `--` in `cargo run -- path`, so cargo tries to parse the path itself.
Not importing the `owo_colors::OwoColorize` trait, which gives 'no method named red' errors.
Using `.unwrap()` instead of `unwrap_or`, which panics when no path is given.
Forgetting `use std::path::PathBuf`.
Writing `Some(does_exist)` instead of `Ok(does_exist)`, because try_exists returns a Result.

steps.title: List directory file names
steps.instructions: Write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that loops over `fs::read_dir(path)` and pushes each entry's `file_name()` as a String (fallback "unknown name"). In main, loop `for file in get_files(&path)` and print each name, then `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Helper returning a Vec<String> of file names
cargo run lists the current directory

explanations.topic: try_exists returns Err when existence can't be confirmed or denied
if let Ok(...) = fs::read_dir(path) to iterate entries safely
file_name() gives an OsString; into_string() returns a Result, so unwrap_or a fallback
cargo run with no argument defaults to the working directory

hints: Create a helper that takes &Path and returns Vec<String>; start with an empty vector and return it.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)` then `for entry in read_dir`, and `if let Ok(file) = entry` for each item.
Push `file.file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())` into the vector.
In main, inside the branch where the path exists, write `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }` and run `cargo run`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`, causing unresolved-name errors.
Passing `path` instead of `&path` to get_files when path is a PathBuf.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so push fails to compile.
Calling `.to_string()` on the OsString (not implemented) instead of `.into_string()`.
Forgetting that into_string returns a Result and pushing it directly without unwrap_or.

steps.title: Collect file metadata into structs
steps.instructions: Add `strum` and define `#[derive(Debug, Display)] enum EntryType { File, Dir }` and `struct FileEntry { name, e_type, len_bytes: u64, modified: String }`; in get_files use `fs::metadata(&file.path())` to fill entries via a `map_data` function. Pretty-print with `{:#?}` and run to see the metadata.

targets.caption: Struct holding each file's metadata
File/Dir enum with strum Display
Pretty-printed metadata output

explanations.topic: Designing a struct to hold file metadata
Why `type` can't be a field name (use e_type)
strum's Display derive to turn enums into strings
fs::metadata returns Result, so use if let Ok
Bug: passing the directory path instead of file.path()

hints: Add strum (with the derive feature) to Cargo.toml, then define an EntryType enum and a FileEntry struct deriving Debug.
Inside the loop over read_dir entries, call fs::metadata(&file.path()) and match it with `if let Ok(meta)`.
Pick the type with meta.is_dir(), the size with meta.len(), and use an empty string for modified for now.
Print the Vec with println!("{:#?}", ...); FileEntry and EntryType both need #[derive(Debug)].
common_mistakes: Naming the field `type`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust.
Passing the directory `path` to fs::metadata instead of `file.path()`, which makes every entry show the directory's metadata.
Forgetting #[derive(Debug)] on FileEntry or EntryType, which makes the {:#?} print fail to compile.
Adding strum without the derive feature (or without strum_macros), so `Display` can't be derived.
Treating fs::metadata as returning an Option (`Some`) instead of a Result (`Ok`).

steps.title: Render a styled colored table
steps.instructions: Add the tabled crate, derive Tabled on FileEntry, build `Table::new(...)` with `Style::rounded()` and Color settings, rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = ...)]`, then `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Build the table from the file entries
Rounded table style
Rename column headers
Table header in output

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does
Applying a table Style
Coloring columns and rows with modify
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename)]

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml (cargo add tabled) and add Tabled to the derive list on FileEntry.
Replace the print loop with let mut table = Table::new(get_files(&path)); then println!("{}", table);
Use table.with(Style::rounded()) and table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN); import Style and Color from tabled::settings and Columns/Rows from tabled::settings::object.
Rename headers with #[tabled(rename = "Type")] above a field; every field type must implement Display, so EntryType needs a Display impl.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to derive Tabled on FileEntry, so Table::new does not compile.
A field type like an enum not implementing Display, which Tabled requires.
Importing Style or Color from the wrong module (tabled has several 'Style' types).
Calling table.with/modify on a non-mut table.
Column index off-by-one: Columns indexes start at 0.

steps.title: Format modified dates with chrono
steps.instructions: Add `chrono` and in map_data use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified()` to convert into `DateTime<Utc>` and `.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()`, else an empty string. Run `cargo run -- src` to see dates in the table.

targets.caption: Convert SystemTime into DateTime<Utc>
Run cargo run -- src to see dates

explanations.topic: Why a date/time crate (chrono) is needed
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>; fallback to empty string
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> with .into()
strftime-style format specifiers for printing dates

hints: Add chrono to [dependencies] in Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add chrono`).
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>; wrap it in `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { ... } else { String::new() }`.
Inside the Ok branch: `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();` then `format!("{}", date.format("%a %b %e %Y"))`.
Add `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};` at the top, then run `cargo run -- src`.
common_mistakes: Naming the binding `mod`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust; use `modi` instead.
Forgetting `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};`, causing 'cannot find type DateTime' errors.
Calling .into() without a type annotation, so the compiler can't infer the target type.
Not adding chrono to Cargo.toml, giving 'unresolved import chrono'.
Returning a &str in one branch and a String in the other; both branches must produce String.

steps.title: Add JSON output flag
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, extract table code into `print_table`, and print `serde_json::to_string(...)` when the flag is set after deriving Serialize. Run `cargo run -- -j` and `cargo run -- --help`.

targets.caption: Clap attribute giving -j and --json
Derive Serialize on FileEntry and EntryType
Table code extracted into its own function
New flag listed in --help

explanations.topic: A bare field isn't a flag until it has the #[arg] attribute
short/long give both -j and --json forms
serde + serde_json for serializing structs to JSON
Serialize must be derived on nested enum too
unwrap_or fallback string when serialization fails

hints: Add a `json: bool` field to Cli with `#[arg(short, long)]` above it, then check `cargo run -- --help`.
Add dependencies: `cargo add serde --features derive` and `cargo add serde_json`.
Derive `Serialize` (use serde::Serialize) on both FileEntry and EntryType; every nested type must be serializable.
In main: `if cli.json { println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())); } else { print_table(path); }`
common_mistakes: Adding `json: bool` without `#[arg(short, long)]`, so clap treats it as a positional/required arg instead of a flag
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on EntryType, causing a trait-bound compile error
Adding serde without the `derive` feature, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` isn't found
Forgetting `--` in `cargo run -- -j`, so cargo receives the flag instead of your program
Passing `get_files(&path)` result without `&` or calling print_table in both branches
